content: The studies included a total of 8,921 patients and were conducted as cross-sectional and cohort studies. The evidence quality was rated as low due to serious concerns about bias and indirectness. Many studies relied on a single biopsy of abnormal lesions, which contributed to the downgrading of evidence quality. The diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) data for HPV testing followed by visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) or colposcopy with biopsy were calculated based on the sensitivity and specificity of the tests, but direct data were unavailable. The data were derived from women with unknown HIV status, and the quality of evidence was not downgraded for indirectness in this context. The sensitivity and specificity estimates for HPV testing and VIA were inconsistent despite similar cut-off values, and this variability could not be explained by study quality. This inconsistency, along with imprecision, led to further downgrading of evidence quality. Wide confidence intervals (CIs) for sensitivity and specificity of HPV testing and VIA, as well as for true positives (TP), true negatives (TN), false positives (FP), and false negatives (FN), could result in different clinical decisions depending on the assumed confidence limits. GRADE evidence was assessed for patient-important outcomes following different screen-and-treat strategies. HPV testing followed by VIA, colposcopy, or other treatments (e.g., cryotherapy, loop electrosurgical excision procedure [LEEP], or cold knife conization [CKC]) was compared to no screening. Outcomes included cervical cancer mortality, incidence, recurrence of CIN2+ (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or higher), undetected CIN2+ (FN), major bleeding, premature delivery, infertility, major infections, minor infections, unnecessary treatment (FP), and cancers detected at first-time screening. For cervical cancer mortality, HPV testing followed by colposcopy and biopsy with CKC or LEEP showed the lowest mortality rates compared to other strategies. HPV testing followed by VIA had higher mortality rates. The incidence of cervical cancer was also lowest with colposcopy and biopsy strategies. Recurrence of CIN2+ was higher in strategies involving VIA compared to colposcopy and biopsy. Undetected CIN2+ cases (FN) were more frequent in VIA-based strategies. Major bleeding was observed in a small proportion of patients treated with CKC, while premature delivery was associated with CKC and LEEP treatments. No data were identified regarding infertility risks after treatment for CIN2+. Major infections were rare but occurred in patients treated with CKC. Minor infections were more common but still infrequent. Unnecessary treatment (FP) was higher in VIA-based strategies compared to colposcopy and biopsy. Cancers detected at first-time screening were more frequent in HPV testing followed by colposcopy and biopsy compared to VIA. The pooled sensitivity of VIA was 69% (95% CI: 54–81), and its specificity was 87% (95% CI: 79–92). For HPV testing, the pooled sensitivity was 95% (95% CI: 84–98), and the specificity was 84% (95% CI: 72–91). The overall quality of evidence (QoE) for these outcomes was rated as very low due to the very low quality of evidence for treatment effects and natural progression data. Assumptions were made for certain outcomes. For example, no cervical cancer mortality was assumed in TN and FP cases. Mortality rates for HIV-positive women were assumed to be the same as for women with unknown HIV status. The incidence of cervical cancer was based on age-standardized rates from Eastern Africa, with assumptions about CIN2+ persistence and regression. Major bleeding and infections were assumed to be zero in TN and FN cases, as these patients were not treated. Premature delivery risks were estimated based on population-level risks and treatment-specific risks. No data were available for infertility risks. Minor infections were assumed to be zero in TN and FN cases, with estimates provided for CKC-treated patients. The studies referenced included cross-sectional and comparative trials evaluating various screening techniques, such as HPV testing, VIA, Pap smears, and colposcopy, in different populations and settings. These studies highlighted the diagnostic accuracy and clinical relevance of these methods, particularly in resource-limited settings.
